title: Conduct or facilitate security audits
summary: Audits provide an independent, criteria-based examination of evidence and controls; their credibility depends on scope, competence, independence, and disciplined follow-through.
outcome: Plan or facilitate an audit with appropriate independence, evidence handling, interviews, sampling, findings, management response, and follow-up.
managerMindset: An audit earns trust through transparent criteria, competent evidence work, and independence—not through a favorable conclusion.

sections.title: Protect audit credibility
sections.body: Establish objective, criteria, scope, period, roles, competence, independence, confidentiality, evidence access, sampling, and communication. Internal, external, and third-party audits may differ in independence and purpose; conflicts must be disclosed and managed. Interviews and documents are evidence only when corroborated and evaluated against criteria.
keyPoints: Independence is relative to the audit objective and reporting relationship.
Criteria must be known and consistently applied.
Management owns remediation; auditors report evidence and conclusions.

sections.title: Close the loop
sections.body: Classify findings, obtain management responses, agree corrective actions and dates, communicate residual risk, and track closure with retest or evidence review. An audit report should distinguish nonconformity, observation, limitation, and accepted risk. Follow-up preserves value after the fieldwork ends.
keyPoints: A finding is not closed because a ticket exists; evidence must show the condition was addressed.
Scope limitations can qualify the opinion.
Recurring findings suggest systemic root cause or ineffective governance.

sections.title: Facilitate audits across enterprise and provider boundaries
sections.body: Internal audits operate within organizational governance; external audits add independence or customer/regulator assurance; third-party audits assess suppliers or attestations outside direct enterprise control. For on-premises, cloud, and hybrid scope, establish evidence rights, inherited controls, subprocessor coverage, locations, sampling populations, confidentiality, and contact paths. Facilitation includes opening meetings, evidence requests, interview coordination, issue escalation, management responses, and follow-up without directing the auditor's conclusion.
keyPoints: A provider report may not cover customer configuration or subprocessor scope.
Audit independence and access constraints must be recorded as limitations.
Facilitating logistics is different from altering evidence or suppressing findings.

workedExamples.title: Supplier assurance audit
workedExamples.situation: A critical provider offers an audit report but refuses customer access to its subprocessor controls.
workedExamples.reasoning: Assess report scope, criteria, period, exceptions, complementary customer controls, and subprocessor coverage. Record the limitation, request alternate evidence or contractual rights, and accept residual risk only through accountable governance.

distinctions.difference: An audit emphasizes independent, systematic examination against criteria; an assessment may be broader, risk-oriented, and less formally independent.
The reporting relationship and independence risk differ; neither label alone guarantees objectivity.

misconceptions.misconception: A third-party audit report transfers accountability to the provider.
misconceptions.correction: The report is evidence with scope and limitations; the organization retains responsibility for its use, controls, and risk decisions.

recallChecks.prompt: What makes an audit conclusion credible?
recallChecks.answer: Competent work, relevant criteria, sufficient evidence, defined scope, and managed independence.
Verified corrective action or an accountable, documented risk decision—not merely a planned ticket.

scenarioSeeds.scenario: An auditor's bonus depends on a clean result for the system owner being audited.
scenarioSeeds.decision: Disclose and remove or mitigate the conflict; preserve independent review.

studyPlan.learn: Study audit independence, criteria, evidence, findings, and follow-up.
studyPlan.connect: Connect audit conclusions to D1 governance and D7 control operation.
studyPlan.apply: Critique a supplier report for scope and complementary controls.
studyPlan.revisit: Explain how a finding transitions from evidence to verified closure.

review.notes: Independent AI review only. Claim evidence, exact content fingerprints, scope checks, visual and memory-map assessments are recorded in knowledge/quality/. No human expert review or exam-readiness claim.

visualLearningContract.teachingQuestion: What makes an audit conclusion credible and what closes a finding?
visualLearningContract.formRationale: Aligned columns make concept meanings, decision criteria and failure consequences explicit and comparable.
visualLearningContract.focalInsight: Audit conclusion is bounded by criteria, scope, period, independence, and sampled evidence.
visualLearningContract.intentionalOmissions: No guarantee a report covers customer responsibility.
visualLearningContract.retrievalPrompt: Third-party SOC excludes subcontractor: what audit limitation report?
visualLearningContract.textFallback:
audit: criteria-based examination. Decision: define period/scope. Failure/example: certificate overreach
audit independence: unbiased evaluator. Decision: manage conflict. Failure/example: operator audit
audit criteria: expected standard. Decision: map control. Failure/example: undefined benchmark
audit evidence: supporting artifact. Decision: test reliability. Failure/example: policy-only
sampling: evidence subset. Decision: justify selection. Failure/example: cherry-pick
follow up: corrective closure. Decision: retest evidence. Failure/example: finding disappears
